name: Arnan
title: Descendant of King David in the post-exilic period
summary: Arnan is a figure known exclusively from the genealogy in 1 Chronicles, where he appears in the listing of King David's descendants through the line of Zerubbabel. He is mentioned as the son of Refa and the father of Obadiah. The passage in 1 Chron 3:19–24 presents textual-critical challenges, since the Hebrew base text and the Septuaginta diverge in several details, and the precise familial connections between Zerubbabel and Arnan are subject to various interpretations. Arnan's role in the biblical narrative is to serve as a genealogical link in the Davidic royal line after the exile—a lineage that was carefully documented, likely motivated by messianic expectations that God's covenant promises to David's house would one day be fulfilled.
roles: genealogical link in the Davidic line

keyEvents.title: Listed in King David's royal genealogy
keyEvents.description: Arnan is mentioned in the genealogy of David's descendants in 1 Chronicles, where he is placed as the son of Refa and father of Obadiah. This family tree documents the Davidic line from King David through Zerubbabel and into the post-exilic period, testifying that the royal lineage was carefully preserved even after the kingdom of Judah had ended.

keyEvents.title: Link in Zerubbabel's descendants
keyEvents.description: As part of the list of Zerubbabel's descendants, Arnan represents continuity in the Davidic family line after the return from Babylon. The genealogy likely reflects messianic expectations connected to the house of David and God's promise of an eternal throne.

footnotes.text: The text in 1 Chron 3:19–24 presents textual-critical challenges. The Hebrew base text (Masoretic Text) and the Septuagint contain partly different readings, and there is uncertainty about how many generations are listed and exactly how the genealogical links relate to one another. Some scholars believe the list covers up to eleven generations after Zerubbabel, while others interpret it as fewer.
The name Arnan (Hebrew: אַרְנָן) has an uncertain etymology but may possibly mean 'swift' or 'lively'. In some manuscript traditions, name forms occur that differ somewhat from the Masoretic form.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 3 are among the most important sources for reconstructing David's dynastic line after the Babylonian exile. They testify that the Davidic line was preserved with great care even after the kingdom of Judah ceased to exist, which likely reflects messianic expectations of a future king from David's lineage.

The post-exilic period (ca. 539–400 BCE) was characterized by the rebuilding of the temple and the reorganization of the Jewish community in Judah under Persian sovereignty. The preservation of genealogies served important functions: documenting tribal affiliation, inheritance rights, connection to temple service, and legitimacy within the royal line.

In rabbinic tradition, David's descendants after the exile played a role in discussions about the exilarchate (resh galuta) – leadership of the Jewish diaspora community in Babylon. Some traditions link the exilarchs' lineage to Zerubbabel and thus indirectly to figures such as Arnan.
